reading.body:
Hawaii's 2026 legislature passed four resolutions asking the state energy office to study how large data centers would affect its electric utilities, ratepayers, natural resources, and climate goals. That is the clearest signal in this data that compute buildout is being treated as an electricity question, not just a technology one.

The pattern across the session is procedural rather than binding. The energy office working group appears in HCR206, SCR95, SR90, and HR196, four separate vehicles for the same request, all dated April 2026. The civil rights commission is asked four times over to examine whether existing anti-discrimination law reaches algorithmic and automated decision systems. The volume of duplicate resolutions suggests lawmakers wanted the study requests on the record in both chambers without attaching enforcement.

On AI itself, the bills are mostly introduced and left there. Roughly a dozen measures titled "Relating To Artificial Intelligence" appear between January 2025 and January 2026, and only HB2137 and SB3001 reached passage. The rest sit at Introduced or Engrossed. The subject matter clusters around literacy curricula, protection of minors, health care use, and a statewide data and AI governance center, which is a governance agenda rather than an infrastructure one.

What this data does not show is whether any data center is proposed in Hawaii, how large, or where it would draw power. The resolutions ask those questions rather than answer them. It also does not show the content of the two AI bills that passed, so the strength of what Hawaii actually enacted cannot be read from the titles alone.
